title: How to Use a Wooden Spurtle for Sourdough Naan Bread
meta_description: Master the art of mixing sourdough naan with a wooden spurtle. Learn step‑by‑step tips, tools, and techniques for perfect, fluffy naan every time.
html:
When you’re mixing sourdough naan, the tool you choose can make the difference between a sticky mess and a smooth, elastic dough. A wooden spurtle – the skinny, tapered stirrer that looks like a cross between a whisk and a spatula – is perfect for handling the high‑hydration batter that naan demands. Below is a practical, hands‑on guide that shows how to use a wooden spurtle for sourdough naan, from starter to skillet.

Why a Wooden Spurtle Beats a Traditional Whisk

Traditional metal whisks are great for thin batters, but they tend to tear gluten strands in a thick, wet dough. A wooden spurtle, especially the 2 PCS Wooden Spurtle & Sourdough Starter Stirrer Set, has a smooth, non‑scratch surface that gently folds the dough while keeping air in the batter. The tapered shape reaches the bottom of any mixing bowl or mason jar, making it ideal for scraping every last bit of starter and flour without bruising the gluten.

Preparing Your Sourdough Starter

Before you even think about the naan batter, you need a healthy, active starter. Here’s a quick routine using the spurtle:

  1. Combine 50 g whole‑grain flour and 50 g water in a clean jar.
  2. Stir vigorously with one side of the wooden spurtle until the mixture is uniform – no dry flour patches.
  3. Cover loosely and let sit at room temperature for 12‑24 hours.
  4. Refresh daily (discard half, feed with equal parts flour and water) until the starter bubbles and doubles in size within 4‑6 hours of feeding.

The slim profile of the spurtle makes it easy to scrape the sides of the jar, ensuring you don’t waste any starter. When the starter is bubbly and aromatic, it’s ready for the naan mix.

Mixing the Sourdough Naan Dough

Now for the star of the show: mixing sourdough naan. The dough is wetter than typical bread dough, so you’ll want a tool that can handle a fluid consistency without splashing.

  • Ingredients (for one batch): 150 g active sourdough starter, 250 g all‑purpose flour, 120 ml warm water, 1 tsp sugar, 1 tsp salt, 2 tbsp melted butter, ½ tsp baking soda.
  • Step‑by‑step:
    1. In a large mixing bowl, whisk together the starter, water, and sugar with the wooden spurtle until the starter dissolves.
    2. Add the flour and salt. Use the spurtle to fold the flour into the liquid, moving in a circular motion. The tapered tip helps pull the dry flour from the sides into the center.
    3. Once a shaggy dough forms, let it rest for 10 minutes (autolyse). This gives the flour time to hydrate and the gluten a head start.
    4. After the rest, add the melted butter and baking soda. Continue mixing with the spurtle, gently folding rather than beating. The dough should become smooth, slightly tacky, and pull away cleanly from the bowl.

The wooden spurtle’s slender shape allows you to work the dough in a bowl without over‑developing gluten, which is crucial for the soft, pillowy texture that naan is known for.

Bulk Fermentation and Shaping

Cover the bowl with a damp towel and let the dough rise at room temperature for 3‑4 hours, or until it has increased by about 50 percent. During the first hour, give the dough a gentle “stretch‑and‑fold” using the spurtle: lift a portion of the dough, stretch it upward, and fold it back onto itself. This reinforces structure without the need for heavy kneading.

When the bulk rise is complete, turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface. Divide it into 6‑8 equal pieces and shape each into a ball. Let the balls rest for 15 minutes – this relaxes the gluten and makes rolling easier.

Rolling and Cooking the Naan

Using a rolling pin, roll each ball into a ¼‑inch‑thick circle. If you prefer a more rustic look, you can stretch the dough by hand, pulling gently from the center outward. Preheat a cast‑iron skillet or heavy‑bottomed pan over medium‑high heat until it’s shimmering.

Place the rolled naan on the hot skillet. Cook for 30‑45 seconds, until bubbles form on the surface, then flip and cook another 30‑seconds on the other side. Brush with melted butter or ghee while it’s still hot. The quick, high heat creates the characteristic char spots and fluffy interior.

Cleaning Up with the Wooden Spurtle

One of the underrated benefits of the 2 PCS Wooden Spurtle & Sourdough Starter Stirrer Set is how easy it is to clean. After you’re finished mixing and scraping the jar, simply rinse the spurtle under warm water and wipe it dry. The wood won’t retain odors, and because it’s non‑scratch, you can use it on silicone, stainless steel, or even non‑stick pans without worrying about damage.

FAQ

Can I use a wooden spurtle for high‑gluten doughs like pizza?

Yes. The spurtle’s gentle folding action works well for any dough that benefits from minimal over‑mixing. For very stiff doughs, you may need a stronger tool, but the spurtle can still be used to incorporate ingredients and scrape bowls.

Is the wooden spurtle safe for dishwasher use?

While the wood is durable, we recommend hand‑washing to preserve the finish and prevent cracking. A quick rinse and a dab of food‑grade oil after drying will keep it in top shape.

How often should I replace my spurtle?

With proper care, a quality wooden spurtle can last years. Look for signs of splintering or a loss of smoothness; when the surface becomes rough, it’s time for a replacement.
